speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Such an amendment to GPA can better protect our troops and better enhance public confidence in SAF in the area of training safety.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I had asked whether this law could be amended at least to reduce the possible moral hazard of any officers not taking sufficient care and caution in abiding by established TSRs during training exercises.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In response, the Minister for Defence said that if I felt strongly about the changes to GPA, I could put up a Motion.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I do feel strongly about not just the case of Pte Lee.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But there are larger issues at stake as well.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They have to do with ensuring that our women and men in uniform have the protection they deserve during training.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This remains the case even as SAF seeks to prepare them realistically for tough operational situations.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They also have to do with bolstering public confidence in the Armed Forces.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: After all, we have an armed forces which is composed mostly of conscripts.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Anything to do with SAF has the potential to affect every single Singaporean family.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As legislators, those of us in this House have an obligation to citizens that we work to their best interests.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is for these reasons that I am moving this Motion.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Tough and realistic training is important for SAF.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, training occurs in a controlled environment by design, unlike operations that, by their nature, have higher levels of risk, uncertainty and unpredictability.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Action and behaviour permissible during training should be subject to more stringent limits than operations.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Managing the training environment ensures that not only learning takes place, but that service personnel do not face unnecessary physical risks.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our Servicemen must remain safe, healthy, fit and ready for operations when called.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: All military training and operations carry some risks to be sure, but training affords the controlled circumstances that allow the careful management of such risks.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The aim is to ensure that learning takes place without harm to our service personnel.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These are the same personnel whom we will have to rely on during operations.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To expect service personnel to risk themselves for our country, to go into harm's way for us when asked, it is only right for the nation to afford them adequate protection where possible, not least during training, when what is at stake is a learning outcome and not an immediate life or death situation.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Given Singapore's limited human resources, it is also in the interest of SAF and the nation to keep injury and death in training to a minimum.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Actually, SAF has always recognised this distinction between training and operations.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: That is precisely why SAF has the TSR and other safety directions in lesson plans.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When I was an officer cadet, we were all drilled in the TSR.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We consulted the TSR and had safety briefings before activities and exercises.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When we go into the units, the same emphasis on TSR remains.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This was also the case during my National Servicemen (NSmen) training.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As NSmen commanders, the safety of our men during training and observance of TSR are always top priorities.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: After all, every NSmen is a son, sibling, spouse or father to another Singaporean.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We inprocess together to do our In Camp Training once a year and we want to outprocess together with everyone safe, sound and happy to go back to our families.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: NSmen who have been through the usual NS cycles will understand that and it is down to NSmen commanders to ensure, as far as training safety is concerned, that that will happen.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The TSRs describe safety procedures in detail, often giving very exact distances, ranges, equipment and contingency safety measures for different types of training exercises.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They lay out what should be done and spell out what needs to be avoided.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A mistake from carelessness, laziness, or irresponsibility may lead to serious injury, even loss of life.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, it is important to remind commanders what to do and what to avoid when conducting training.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Lesson plans and TSRs are, in a number of cases, written in blood.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Safety procedures for prisoner of war training saw a revision after the unfortunate death of one service personnel and serious injury to another.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There are other examples which I do not have the time to go into now.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Training situations are and should remain qualitatively different from operational circumstances.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is important not to conflate these very different situations.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Operations are not, at their core, meant for practice and learning.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What is at stake in operations is very different from a training exercise.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They may involve conditions outside the control of commanders and SAF.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In this regard, considerations of risk during operations are very different from training.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is a different case to be made for exempting commanders from legal liability during operational situations.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Training safety protocols obviously do not readily apply.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A clear line exists between operations and training.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I was a little bit surprised when the Minister for Defence equated examples of operations with breaches of safety protocol during training in his reply to my supplementary question in Parliament last March.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Minister cited examples of: (a) a Police Officer discharging a firearm when in pursuit of a suspect that the officer "thinks is going to commit harm"; (b) service personnel who "see a significant threat" at a key installation they are protecting; and, (c) the Police shooting incident after a vehicle tried to breach the barricades at last year's Shangri-La Dialogue and was shot by a Gurkha Police Officer.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Minister's examples all pertain to Police operations, not even training.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Training personnel to make operational decisions does not involve completely replicating a real-world situation.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is peculiar at best to think that training personnel to make snap judgements about responding to significant threats or vehicles breaching barricades requires the use of live weapons on real people, for instance.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A line can and should be drawn between training and operational considerations.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is a line that is clear in principle and in fact.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the Minister's response to my Parliamentary Question in March, he said, "injuries and deaths can happen despite best efforts." He went on to discuss two accidents that involved negligence, a rash act, and an attempt to "pervert the course of justice".

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These incidents involved "acts that amount to criminal offences under general law", as the Minister noted.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I agree with the Minister that accidents can and do sadly occur.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Accidents, however, can take place for a variety of reasons, under a range of conditions.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They may occur on the road, in the regular operation of equipment, or because of unforeseen circumstances.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In training situations, safety protocols laid out in lesson plans and the TSR seek to minimise accidents and other incidents.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There may be situations that are not criminal but where victims and their families should still be able to seek legal recourse directly.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am not calling for a blanket civil liability for accidents; just for accidents during the controlled environment of training.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Training conditions have clear safety codes laid out, and commanders have a duty to comply.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: SAF should not tolerate, much less condone, such behaviour, and it is important to make this clear both within its ranks and to the public.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If commanders choose to engage in such behaviour, if they choose to endanger our children, siblings, spouses or parents in situations that do not warrant such risk, they should answer for it, and not just to the state, but to the Servicemen or to his or her family.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If someone endangers or, worse, harms our women and men in uniform because of a lack of care with regard to established safety protocols, they need to answer to those they have a responsibility for.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This should be the case, even if an act is not criminal.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Answering to SAF through the military justice system does not achieve this.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In effect, at least from a civil law perspective, errant officers or instructors are not directly accountable to the people they are in charge of.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: At best, officers are only accountable to the Ministry of Defence (MINDEF) or to the state.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Minister for Defence is right to say that civil suit is not trivial.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: That is precisely why there are circumstances where civil claims should be allowed, and I submit that violation of safety procedures during the controlled environment of training should be one of them.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Knowledge of the potential seriousness of consequences can encourage those responsible for the lives of our women and men in uniform to be more careful and treat their duties more seriously and be less cavalier about non observance of TSRs or safety considerations in lesson plans.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One common claim about the Singapore legal system is that clear, consistent and proportional sanction deters violations of the law.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Allowing civil liability for violations of training protocol is an extension of this principle.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The point about deterrence is that civil liability can be quite easily avoided by adherence to established safety regulations governing the type of training in question.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Even if an accident happens, and they unfortunately do, once commanders have shown that they have taken all necessary precautions and have complied with TSR requirements, they should not be held responsible.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They should not have to worry about any civil liability.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Minister has, in response to my supplementary question about lifting the right to sue for training cases, said that: "The Member says, why not lift it from training?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: You cannot train at one pace and expect your security forces to ramp up their capabilities when in real operations.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is a saying, you know, 'When you do not sweat in training, you will spill blood in real operations'.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: You have to make your training realistic so that when we meet those circumstances – like the guard who fired at the car and stopped the car in time.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Do you think you can get that level of proficiency if they think they are not protected during training?" With respect, I was not asking for unbridled or unrealistic restrictions to training.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: That is quite clear from the scenarios I cited in my question.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Surely, the Minister was not implying that training in compliance with TSRs is not realistic or that any breaches of TSRs to make training realistic is acceptable to SAF.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Minister mentioned that punitive actions have, in the past, been taken against errant officers by way of criminal proceedings or proceedings under military law.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: By military law, it can, of course, be Court Martial proceedings or summary trials.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But such actions are very different from the rights of an injured Serviceman or the family of a deceased Serviceman having to commence a civil claim in negligence against any errant officer or SAF.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Serviceman or his family has no say whether criminal proceedings, Court Martial proceedings or summary trials are to be commenced.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is completely at the discretion of MINDEF or the Attorney-General's Chambers.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is unlike the right to a civil claim, where the decision to commence action lies with a Serviceman or his family.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: By allowing them to have the right of suit, once the suit is commenced, the Courts will decide on liability based on the evidence and arguments that are presented before it.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The defendants have the right to defend themselves.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The injured Serviceman or the family of the Serviceman bringing the suit still has the burden to prove his or their case, as is required for all civil cases.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Ultimately, it is up to the civil Courts to decide based on the merits of the case.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It appears that the offer was "based on the full extent allowed by the compensation legislation".

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I have two further reservations about this system of compensation.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This seems to be strictly on a confidential and "without prejudice" basis.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While as a lawyer I have familiarity with this kind of thinking in litigation, for the lay person without having the right of civil suit, the entire culture of this internal system of compensation to have offers couched in confidential, "without prejudice" language and with MINDEF's denial of liability as a basis for such compensation, just does not augur well for the confidence of the injured Serviceman or the family of a deceased Serviceman in such a system.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Above all, the availability of such offers of compensation does not, in itself, encourage officers to comply with TSRs.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Allowing civil proceedings is not about pinning guilt on particular individuals, which is ironically the case with the current regimes used by MINDEF, such as summary trial, Court Martial or criminal proceedings.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: It is about giving a Serviceman or his family an unfettered right of recourse not dependent on an organisation which might otherwise have been vicariously liable for the tort but for the current statutory exemption from liability.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Such an amendment helps to enhance adherence to training safety protocols and bolster public confidence in SAF.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: We can and should always strive to do better.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: This includes enhancing training, which includes more attention to promoting safety for our troops.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: It also involves taking steps that further bolster public confidence in SAF as a key national institution.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: But as we all know, unfortunately, despite our best efforts, mishaps do occur from time to time.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: When these safety breaches do occur, we want to make sure that those responsible are punished.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: And we certainly do not condone these acts.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: It is not fair to paint even those who have not followed TSRs, as some do it out of mischief or negligence, and they are taken to task if they are reckless.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Some do it for a variety of reasons, so there is a spectrum.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: But if they have been reckless or negligent, they are not protected from criminal prosecution, even when they are conducted by Servicemen in the course of duty.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The Coroner's Inquiry for fatalities is an open process.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: He did mention that we changed the smoke grenade, but he did not say the reason why.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Because it was an acute hypersensitive reaction, which is very uncommon.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: So, I think the facts are established by an independent body.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: If there is criminal negligence and rash acts, they are charged in criminal Courts and punished accordingly.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Members can refer to our records, which I will not repeat here.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Apart from criminal proceedings, SAF and its members can be litigated against for compensation in the civil Courts for damage done to civil property or injury suffered by civilians.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The Member is quite right in raising section 14, that section 14 exempts the Government and servicemen from being sued.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: I thought it would be useful, in response to the Member's various points, to quote the Grounds of Decision (GDs) by Judicial Commissioner (JC) Kannan Ramesh in this specific case which he cited, the Estate of Lee Rui Feng Dominique Sarron, deceased v Najib Hanuk bin Muhammad Jalal.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: And in the GD, the judge provided a comprehensive examination of the history and the reasons for section 14 and I will share some passages.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The judge recognised that section 14 of the GPA was enacted to place SAF in a special position in recognition of its heavy responsibility of safeguarding the defence of our country and the high degree of risk intrinsic to military training. "Intrinsic to military training".

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: JC Kannan added that the consistent legislative intention underpinning section 14 is to ensure that the Government and the members of the Armed Forces are shielded from liability in tort in order to ensure the efficiency, discipline, effectiveness and decisiveness of the Armed Forces in both training and operations, without being burdened by the prospect of legal action when training, to the point of having to second guess the consequences of every action.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The Member paints it as if this Act protects the Government and Servicemen who are not part of our Singapore community.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: But he is absolutely correct that we are a conscript army and this very Act protects commanders and Servicemen who are also partly drawn from our Singaporean community.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Each country will have to decide how it provides its public security agencies as a whole and their personnel − in our case, the SAF, Singapore Police Force and Singapore Civil Defence Force − the confidence to train and perform their duties diligently without this fear of litigation against them.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Note that section 14 does not accord any of our Servicemen any protection against criminal proceedings or civil litigations brought by civilians for compensation or damages, which I have already stated earlier.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: It only precludes legal suits brought against the Government − the SAF in this case − or its individual Servicemen by Servicemen and their next of kin themselves.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Note, as JC Kannan highlighted, that the immunity conferred by section 14 does not extend to acts that amount to an intentional act committed by an SAF member, which is separate and independent of the member's duties, for instance, punching his superior.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: For Singapore, section 14 continues to serve a vital purpose as intended.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: SAF soldiers train realistically, conduct many operations overseas.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Because they train realistically, without the commanders or the individual soldiers themselves in each instance wondering if their organisation or they themselves could be sued by other Servicemen, when injuries and fatalities occur.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Removing section 14 is not likely to improve outcomes, as the Member says and, indeed, may do us harm.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: But in a 2013 report published by the UK House of Commons' Defence Committee, it was found that repealing that protection had resulted in reputational risk to armed forces personnel and the fear that they and their legitimate actions may be exposed to extensive and retrospective legal scrutiny.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: This had led many to question their position serving in the UK armed forces.
